title: Anybody Headed Down Today?
intro: Sunday morning, and Priya's out front of Middle Brook Cafe in Jefferson, checking her phone every few minutes between customers.
smallTalk: Priya's boy has a showcase in the city tonight. Half the village knows already.
Walt's truck is on J&H's lot with the hood up.
The trail's dry the whole way to Hobart this week.
Tops has the good peaches in.
Soggiest summer anybody up here can remember.
Nice to see everybody pitching in for Priya's boy.
Somebody's fixing up the space under Stamford Coffee. Nobody will say what.
Stamford Coffee has a record on this morning.
The self-serve fridge at Stamford Coffee has dinner in it, if you're late home.
80 Main has the Catskills sweaters in again.

items.name: Priya's costume bag
items.blurb: Half a dance costume, sequins and all.

items.name: Jess R.'s jumper cables
items.blurb: Red and black, coiled neat, out of the back of her truck.

lines: It got there? He sent me a photo from the stage door. Sequins and all.
Thank you.
Those are Jess R.'s cables, aren't they? Good. Walt will know what to do with them.
Walt's battery is dead? That truck.
Somebody round here will have cables. Half the village keeps a set.
Did you find Walt? He's up at J&H, on the corner. You'll see the green pickup before you see him.
Sorry — I keep looking at the road. My son's dance showcase is in the city tonight, and half his costume is in this bag. I left it out of his case this morning.
I'm on the register till four, and it's three hours down. He needs it by five.
Walt goes down every other Sunday. He's up at J&H with his truck. If you're walking that way, would you take it to him?
You found cables? Good. Now I need a car with a good battery parked next to mine, running, ten minutes or so.
Any of the Jesses would do it, if you can find one.
No luck yet? Still dead.
Cables first. Then a car with a good battery next to mine for ten minutes.
Priya's bag? Sure, I'll take it down. I go every other Sunday. Put it on the seat.
Only I'm not going anywhere yet. Battery's dead, and my cables are hanging in the garage at home.
If you come across anyone with a set, send them over. It's usually a Jess who bails me out — there are four of them round here, and I always ask the wrong one first.
The truck? Battery's dead. I'm waiting on a jump.
Walt got his jump? Good. Jess R. will want those cables back before he forgets whose they are.
Those are Jess R.'s cables. She'd lend them to anyone.
Jess R.? Try the south end of the trail, where the old rail bed starts. She'll have a pack on.
Walt's battery? Again.
Jess R. keeps cables in her truck. She went past here at eight with a pack on, headed for the trail.
Morning. Waiting on the mail, same as every day.
He got it started? Good. I'll get the cables back off him sometime.
You've got them. Go on — I've eleven miles to walk.
Cables? For Walt? I've a set in the truck. Here.
Give them back whenever. He knows where I am.

effects.toast: You've got Jess R.'s jumper cables.

lines: The rail trail? Eleven miles to Hobart and not a hill on it. I'll be there by lunch.
You can hear the creek most of the way.
The truck's away? Told you. Ten minutes.
Walt got his jump? That's all that truck ever wants.
Those will do. Now he needs a running car next to his.
Walt's truck? Cables, and a car with a good battery. Ten minutes.
Walt's green pickup? I've had my head under that hood.
Cables on their own won't start it. He needs another car next to his with a good battery, running, ten minutes at least.
This spot? Best one in Hobart. The water does all the talking.
Walt? Ten minutes and it turned over. That's all it ever was.
Sit tight. It wants a good ten minutes.
You've got cables? Then I've got the car. The wagon's over on the gas station lot, and it starts first turn.
Come on.
Walt's battery? I'd pull the wagon over now, only I've no cables either.
Mine went with a car I sold in April.
Me? Coffee on the patio and nothing I have to do.
My wagon's over on the gas station lot. I walked across.
Did the bag make it? Tell me it made the stage door.
Those are Jess R.'s cables. She'll not want them back in a hurry.
Walt needs a jump? Then he'll want one of the Jesses.
Somebody in here this morning said one of them was headed up to him already.
Priya's bag? Walt's the one who goes down. Every other Sunday, regular as the mail.
Morning! Coffee's on, and yes, the sundae bar's real.
Priya was on the phone in here earlier, asking around about getting something down to the city tonight.
It worked out? Good. Come by for a tasting sometime.
Jess R.'s cables? Good. She never minds lending them.
Walt needs a jump? I'd go up myself if my truck weren't in the shop.
Jess T., by the bridge, had her own hood up half of last winter. She'll know what that truck needs.
A ride to the city? Not me today — my truck's in the shop. Walt goes down every other Sunday. He's the one.
Welcome. Pull up a seat on the bench any time.
Walt got away? Good. Tell Priya's boy break a leg from all of us in here.
Walt's battery? Somebody came in saying so. He'll be fine — nobody's stuck for long round here.
Downstairs? Still no idea.
Downstairs? Still no idea. There's paper over the window. I've looked anyway.
Sit anywhere. You can hear the record player from every table.
Have you heard about the space underneath us? Somebody's been hammering down there all week. Nobody knows what it is — I've asked at the counter twice.
If I had to guess, a gallery. Half the people at these tables paint.
Downstairs? Nobody knows and everybody's got a theory. I say oysters.
Whoever it is, they've picked a good spot.
Don't mind me — I'm deciding between two sweaters and losing.
The work under the coffee shop? The whole town's noticed. Nobody knows what it is.
My guess is an oyster bar. The wine nights in here fill right up.
Downstairs? Still no answer. I'm still saying dog treats.
He sniffs at that window every single walk.
Morning. Biscuit checks the patio before we go anywhere, so we check the patio.
The space under the coffee shop? Somebody's doing it up. Paper on the window and hammering behind it, and that's all anybody knows.
My guess is dog treats. Every dog in Stamford naps on this deck.
Red to red, black on the bracket. Now leave it running.
Ten minutes. I'll drink my coffee.
There it is. Listen to that.
Thank you, Jess. I'd have asked you first, only I never can keep the four of you straight.

steps.toast: Episode complete — new story next week

lines: Taped inside the door: "The truck on the lot is Walt's. He's waiting on a jump."
Pinned to the board by the door: somebody's asking if anybody's headed down to the city tonight. Two people have written "ask Walt" underneath, in two different pens.
Down the side of the coffee shop, a low window right at the ground, with brown paper and a sheet of plywood over it from the inside. Somebody is at work behind it — you can hear a saw.
Not a word written on any of it.
